questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Cartesian Form
questions.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=7\,i+2\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=36.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $6.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =7, \\ Q(x,y) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(7)\cdot (6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(2)\cdot (-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }42\operatorname{cos}⁡t+12\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(42\operatorname{sin}⁡t-12\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =(0-12)-(0-12) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=8\,i-(x+3)\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={2}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $2.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =8, \\ Q(x,y) & =x+3=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the double-angle formula for sine, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(8)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(16\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074644/assets/0ea0204d3e1f230efcde4b82da36b1986af732cdf2a01ad868aa0f6bf7414326.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=4y\,i+(2x-1)\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [0,1],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074644/assets/59e503e0c4d950f030891bbaeb7ed890426ef470a1e1dae89d27eabb8dd591a6.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2},\,y=t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =4y=4t, \\ Q(x,y) & =2x-1=2{t}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4t)\cdot (1)-(2{t}^{2}-1)\cdot (2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4t-4{t}^{3}+2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6t-4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}-{t}^{4}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(3-1)-(0-0){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074644/assets/6043a1f88474e2c282938d3b3f0193002b6e11b5fb6d16292fea43d63292d1b0.png)

The curve $C$ is given by $y={x}^{3}$ from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(1,1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=-3{x}^{2}\,i+\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y={t}^{3},\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(1,1).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074644/assets/1d54fe3c07f04a7d05567942e3eea6efaf1cb516070a5d7cc31ef726c0ddb423.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-3{x}^{2}=-3{t}^{2}, \\ Q(x,y) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})=3{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-3{t}^{2})\cdot (3{t}^{2})-(1)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-9{t}^{4}-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-\frac{9{t}^{5}}{5}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(-\frac{9}{5}-1)-0 \\  & =-\frac{14}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074644/assets/67dca8f0202d0c5d1041935a6aee7c4ebd0e3c6c449f2ee1a5ff24c1f381410c.png)

The curve $C$ is given by $x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ from the point $(1,\frac{1}{e})$ to the point $(0,1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=2{y}^{2}\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,y=t,\,t\in [\frac{1}{e},1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(1,\frac{1}{e})$ to the point $(0,1).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074644/assets/08fc4561a322b690da7bd28a9e69a91c687256e8a902ec7690dda5e6a1c689a6.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =0, \\ Q(x,y) & =2{y}^{2}=2{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{ln}⁡t)=-\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}(0)\cdot (1)-(2{t}^{2})\cdot (-\frac{1}{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =({t}^{2}){|}_{1/e}^{1} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$
